job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Wei Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did electronic engineering at Cardiff and started in October as a junior embedded engineer at a company near Newport that makes sensors for car engines. I write the small programs that run on the chips, I test boards on a bench, and I attend a morning stand-up where I say about three sentences. I rent a room in Newport with a guy from work, and every Sunday I'm at my parents' restaurant helping wash up and doing the books on my laptop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the bench, when a board that's been dead for two days suddenly blinks. What wears me out is Sundays at the restaurant after a six-day week, because I love my parents but it's a lot. I owe about 18,000, and I send my mum 100 a month when the restaurant is quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's fine. I use an AI chat tool now and then to explain a datasheet, and it's useful, but it's not magic. Hard work still beats hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel a bit relieved but my head would still be full of the restaurant. Food costs and energy keep going up, and my parents' lease comes up for renewal next year. My own job is safe, but the family money is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, put 150 a month to the loan and 100 to my mum, and go on helping at the restaurant on Sundays. I'd also check whether I could get a small raise if I take on the board-testing duties. I'd not take any risks with money right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. Not because of machines, but because of the lease.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the lease goes up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would try to cut a staff member, which means my mum works more hours. I'd probably send 250 a month instead of 100 and eat at home. It's what you do for your parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have they asked you to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. My dad would be offended if I offered. I'd just leave an envelope in the kitchen drawer and not say anything.

say: I'd say that's fine, and **hard work** still beats hype.
I use AI for datasheets, but it's **not magic**.
think: Privately my head is full of the **restaurant**, with food costs and a lease renewal due next year.
My own job is safe, but the **family money** is not.
do: Pay **150 a month** to the loan and 100 to my mum, and keep helping on Sundays.
Ask about a small **raise** for taking on board-testing duties.
feel: A bit **heavy**, not because of machines but because of the lease.
S0.quote: I'd just leave an envelope in the kitchen drawer and not say anything.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **family restaurant**, not AI, and he supports his parents without being asked.
He sends money quietly because his father would be **offended** by an offer.
Say and think are close; the weight shows only in private.

steps.text: Keep working on the board testing at the sensor company
Pay 150 a month towards the loan
Leave an envelope with 100 for my mum each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's strong but we've seen big changes before. I'd say people who work hard and keep learning will be fine, and the government should stay out of the way. I'd tell my coworkers to try the tools now and then to see where they help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel a bit more worried. Embedded coding and testing is exactly the kind of work that AI can speed up, so maybe the company hires half as many juniors. I'm steady, so I'd rather be in the middle of the pack than first or last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly on my own time, because the company will want it. I'd also ask to work on hardware tasks, like board bring-up, where you need to touch the thing. And I'd put more away, since I don't want my parents' money problems and my own at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I think I'd be fine. It feels like climbing a hill I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not just trust the company to look after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Companies look after companies. I don't blame them, that's what they're for, but I'd rather rely on my own skill and my family than on a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think a union would help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not against them, but I wouldn't join first. In my experience, the people who do well are the ones who make themselves useful, and I'd trust that over a meeting.

say: I'd say people who **keep learning** will be fine.
I'd tell coworkers to try the tools and see where they **help**.
think: Embedded coding and testing is what AI speeds up, so the company may hire **half as many juniors**.
I'd rather be in the **middle of the pack** than first or last.
do: Learn the tools on my own time and ask for **hardware tasks** like board bring-up.
Save more so family money problems don't hit at the **same time** as mine.
feel: **Uneasy**, but I think I'd be fine, like climbing a hill I know.
S1.quote: I'd rather rely on my own skill and my family than on a boss.
fieldNote: He distrusts both **companies and unions** and trusts skill and family, a clear traditional outlook.
He picks **hardware tasks** because touching the board is the hardest to automate.
The mood is uneasy, not anxious, because he sees a path.

steps.text: Learn the AI coding tool properly in the evenings
Ask to work on board bring-up and bench testing
Save an extra 100 a month for a family buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is not enough, and I'd want families and firms to hold together. I wouldn't say much online, because I don't think shouting helps. I'd say we should look after each other first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be alarmed. If AI can do almost any thinking work in 2028, my job and half the engineers I know are done. Robots come in 2031 for hands-on work, but the board-testing jobs would go then too. And I'm the one my parents rely on if the restaurant fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost, move back into my parents' flat above the restaurant, and work there full-time if I have to. The restaurant has hands-on work that robots won't do for years, and my parents trust me. I'd talk to my uncle, who runs a small building firm, about a trade for the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be doing sums at night, and I'd hide it at the family table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents know about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They know I make sensors and that I'm paid fairly. My dad says it's a good clean job, and I'd hate to tell him it might not last. I'd tell him slowly, and with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to the restaurant full-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. It's hard work, but it's honest, and I'd be useful there. My mother would cry, and then she'd put me on the till.

say: I'd say two years is not enough and **families and firms** should hold together.
I wouldn't **shout** online; I'd say we look after each other first.
think: If AI does almost any thinking work in 2028, my job and half the engineers I know are **done**.
I'm the one my parents rely on if the **restaurant** fails.
do: Move into my parents' flat above the **restaurant** and cut every cost.
Ask my **uncle**, who runs a small building firm, about a trade for the long run.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd be doing sums at night and hiding it at the family table.
S2.quote: My dad says it's a good clean job, and I'd hate to tell him it might not last.
fieldNote: He worries about letting his **parents down**, not only losing the job, and would hide it from them.
The restaurant is a **fallback and a duty** at once.
His uncle's building firm shows he thinks about hands-on trades.

steps.text: Move into my parents' flat above the restaurant
Cut every cost except the loan payment and my mum's 100
Ask my uncle about a trade apprenticeship at his building firm
Tell my parents slowly and agree a family plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare if you start soon. I'd say people should save and pick up a trade or a skill, and not wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious but not afraid. By 2031 I'd be 27, and I could have paid my loan and put something into my parents' restaurant. Hands-on jobs have three more years, so I'd like a skill that sits between the electronics and the physical world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for a role that installs and maintains sensors and machines, not only writes code. I'd save 400 a month for the restaurant's lease and the loan. And I'd ask my dad if we could add an online ordering system and a small delivery service before the market changes, because I can build that myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Five years feels like what you'd give a young person to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the online ordering for your parents or for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For them first, but if it works it's a little business I can grow. A restaurant is a lot of work for one family, and I'd like to make it a bit less hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say we've always done it with a notepad. Then he'd ask how much it costs. I'd tell him it's free to try, and he'd allow me one month.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to prepare, and people should **save and learn**.
I'd say nobody should wait to be **rescued**.
think: By 2031 I'd be 27 and could have paid my loan and **helped the restaurant**.
I want a skill between the electronics and the **physical world**.
do: Aim for a role that **installs and maintains** sensors and machines.
Save **400 a month** and build online ordering for my parents' restaurant.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan; five years is enough to build something.
S3.quote: A restaurant is a lot of work for one family, and I'd like to make it a bit less hard.
fieldNote: His plan blends his **electronics skill** with the family restaurant, which is inventive and loyal.
His father's notepad answer shows the **generation gap** gently.
He stays anxious because the restaurant's money and his job are tied together.

steps.text: Apply for an installation and maintenance role for sensors and machines
Save 400 a month for the lease and the loan
Build an online ordering page for the restaurant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. It's long enough for people to learn, adapt and sort out the rules. I'd say let the market work and let families look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married, maybe with a child, and paying off a mortgage. I could also have the restaurant doing well with online orders and something extra on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at the sensor firm and move into a senior role, finish paying off the loan within four years, and save for a flat. I'd help my parents modernise the restaurant, and I'd keep learning the tools the way I do now, when others have proved them. I'd also be giving money to my parents' pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit hopeful. This is the one where I get to be a son and an engineer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you from feeling calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big firms get all the gains and small restaurants and small firms are left out. I'm not for handouts, but I'd want a fair market, so a family business can still compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think that will happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Nobody does. That's why I'd rather save now and keep something in reserve than assume it will be fine.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, long enough to learn and adapt.
I'd say let the **market work** and families look after their own.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, probably married, and could have the **restaurant** doing well.
I'd want a **fair market**, so a family business can still compete.
do: Move into a **senior role**, clear the loan in four years and save for a flat.
Help my parents **modernise** the restaurant and put money into their pension.
feel: **Calm** and a bit hopeful; I get to be a son and an engineer.
S4.quote: I'd rather save now and keep something in reserve than assume it will be fine.
fieldNote: He is calm only when the **family business** and his own career both look safe.
His one condition is a **fair market**, not handouts, which fits his outlook.
He admits nobody knows how it will go and treats savings as his insurance.

steps.text: Work towards a senior engineer role at the sensor firm
Clear the student loan within four years
Save a deposit for a flat and plan to marry
Put money into modernising the restaurant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time to look after my parents and I'd be doing it all at once. What would help is a steady job for a few more years, my family close, and a chance to learn a skill that's still needed. A fair market so small family businesses can survive helps too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think engineers are all alone with a laptop. Mine is a family, and the family comes first.

headlineQuote: Mine is a family, and the family comes first.
portrait: Wei is a 22-year-old **electronic engineer** in his first job at a car-sensor company near Newport, owing about 18,000.
He is steady, uses an **AI tool** now and then, and learns new tools once others have proved them.
His traditional, free-market outlook favours hard work and **family** over handouts or union meetings.
His main pressure is his parents' restaurant; he is uneasy at the plateau, alarmed at two years and **calm** at ten.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because he'd have no time to look after his parents and would face everything at once.
whatWouldHelp: A steady job for a few years, a **fair market** for small family firms, and a skill that's still needed.
